result:
Moss has no roots, technically speaking—only rhizoids, tiny threads that anchor without feeding. It drinks directly from the air, from fog and dew, absorbing moisture across its entire surface like a creature that decided to become its own sponge. That's why it thrives where other plants surrender: stone walls, shaded bricks, the north side of trees, forgotten rooftops. It doesn't need much. It never has.

Mosses were among the first plants to leave the water and colonize land, some 450 million years ago. Before forests, before flowers, before any landscape we'd recognize, there was moss—a green film creeping over bare rock, dying and decomposing in slow motion until it became soil. Every forest floor you've ever walked on exists because of that patient labor. In a sense, moss built the ground beneath the trees.

And still we barely notice it. We call a lawn unkempt when moss appears, treating an older, humbler success as if it were a failure. It asks for nothing: no mowing, no fertilizer, no rich earth. When drought comes, it simply stops—drying into a brittle brown crust that looks dead for months, then greening within hours of rain. Botanists call this poikilohydry. I think of it as patience perfected.

There's probably a lesson in that, though I'm wary of lessons drawn from plants. Even so: moss persists not by conquering but by enduring, not by growing tall but by growing everywhere. It covers the world quietly, one damp stone at a time, asking only that someone occasionally look down.
